Tutorials 01: Fundamentals

Tutorial 01.05: Maths examples

This tutorial gives a list of examples of mathematical and arithmentic functions.

See the full list for more info.

As in the previous tutorial you can copy and paste each of these examples to replace the entire body of the constructGraph() function.

Aritmetic operators: as already illustrated, these construct processing units based on the mathematical signal. As such the + operator can mix signals and the * operator can amplify/attenuate signals. This example takes a signal in the ±1 range and maps it between 220...880 using multiply and add (or scale and offset).

    UGen mod = SinOsc::AR(1);
    mod = mod * 330 + 550;
    UGen output = SinOsc::AR(mod, 0, 0.2);
    return output;

There are convenience UGens for this kind of common operation as illustrated in the previous tutorial. LinLin performs a mapping from one linear range to another linear range. This is equivalent to the previous example.

     UGen mod = SinOsc::AR(1);
     mod = LinLin::AR(mod, -1, 1, 220, 880);
     UGen output = SinOsc::AR(mod, 0, 0.2);
     return output;

The UGen class has some of these "mapping" UGens built in as convenience functions. Again this is identical to the above:

     UGen mod = SinOsc::AR(1).linlin(-1, 1, 220, 880);
     UGen output = SinOsc::AR(mod, 0, 0.2);
     return output;

Exponential mapping is often more appropriate for mapping a linear range to control frequency. Using linear mapping the midpoint is 550Hz (halfway between 220 and 880). However, it would be more musical to have 440Hz as the midpoint since this is an octave above the lower bound (double 220Hz) AND an octave below the upper bound (half 880Hz).

     UGen mod = SinOsc::AR(1);
     mod = LinExp::AR(mod, -1, 1, 220, 880); // or use .linexp(...)
     UGen output = SinOsc::AR(mod, 0, 0.2);
     return output;

In fact we could generate this modulator in the MIDI note range then convert it to frequency to achieve the same effect. Here 220Hz is MIDI note 57 and 880Hz is MIDI note 81.

     UGen mod = SinOsc::AR(1).linlin(-1, 1, 57, 81);
     UGen output = SinOsc::AR(mod.midicps(), 0, 0.2);
     return output;

The midicps() function is just one example of the unary operators in UGen++. We could synthesise a sine wave by generating a sawtooth wave a phasor in the ±pi range then applying a sin() function (the SinOsc UGen uses a lookup table rather than calculating the sine function for each sample). This also shows that the constant pi which is defined as part of UGen++.

     UGen output = LFSaw::AR(440, 0, pi).sin();
     return output;

The unary operators can be used in the style above by passing them as a message to a UGen. Or they can be called like a regular function. You can use whichever style you prefer. The message passing style is often more flexible (since you can chain together processes quite easily without ending up with a deeply nested set of parentheses) although might seem unusual to use at first.

     UGen output = sin( LFSaw::AR(440, 0, pi) );
     return output;

Take this example which uses the modulation technique from examples above but quantises pitch to the nearest MIDI note before converting to frequency:

     UGen mod = SinOsc::AR(0.25).linlin(-1, 1, 57, 81).round(1).midicps();
     UGen output = SinOsc::AR(mod, 0, 0.2);
     return output;

Using the functional style the modulator definition would look like this (unless split onto separate lines):

     UGen mod = midicps(round(LinLin::AR(SinOsc::AR(0.25), -1, 1, 57, 81), 1));
     UGen output = SinOsc::AR(mod, 0, 0.2);
     return output;

Splitting onto separate lines is no less efficient when it comes to perform and render the audio. This is because all you are doing at this stage is specifying the interconnections of UGens in to a graph. The example above could become:

    UGen mod = SinOsc::AR(0.25);
    mod = LinLin::AR(mod, -1, 1, 57, 81);
    mod = round(mod, 1);
    mod = midicps(mod);
    UGen output = SinOsc::AR(mod, 0, 0.2);
    return output;

As you can see the separate lines approach is reads in a similar way to the message passing approach.

Comparison operators on UGens produce a signal with binary values 0.0 and 1.0 evaluated for each corresponding sample in the input signals.

e.g., square wave from a sine wave: 

    UGen sine = SinOsc::AR(200, 0, 1.0);
    UGen square = sine > 0.0;       // 0...1 square wave
    UGen output = square.linlin(0, 1, -1, 1);
    output *= 0.2; // amplitude
    return output;

Here when the sine wave is greater than 0.0 the comparison yields 1.0, otherwise it is 0.0 . This example also shows the use of the compound operator *= which works as expected on UGens in the way it works with simple numercial values.
